title: The Mayflower Compact
text:
In November 1620, after more than two months at sea, the Mayflower reached Cape Cod. Its passengers held a patent to settle in the territory of the Virginia Company, far to the south, but bad weather and dangerous shoals forced them to stay where they were. That raised a problem. Outside the area of their patent, no one had legal authority over the colony.

The passengers were a mixed group: religious Separatists from England and the Netherlands, and others recruited for the venture whom the Separatists called "strangers." William Bradford, later the colony's governor, wrote in Of Plymouth Plantation that some of the strangers made discontented and mutinous speeches, saying that once ashore they would use their own liberty, since no one had power to command them.

Before anyone landed, on 11 November by the calendar they used, forty-one men signed a short agreement. They combined themselves, it said, into a "civil body politic," and promised to make and obey just and equal laws for the general good of the colony. They then chose John Carver as their governor.

The first winter was brutal, and about half the colonists died. But the colony held together. The compact remained the basis of Plymouth's government, and later generations saw it as an early example of people agreeing to govern themselves by consent.
lesson: A group heading into uncertainty should agree on its rules before trouble starts. A simple shared commitment can keep a mixed team from splitting apart.
people: William Bradford, John Carver, Mayflower passengers
source: The Mayflower Compact (1620); William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, book 2
